As high as 20.3 percent of all families in Harrisburg have incomes less than 125 percent of the poverty level income, while only 6.2 percent of the families in the urban balance are below 125 percent of the poverty level.
Indications are that this downward trend in income levels (per capita) has been arrested. However, the areas per capita income has been growing less quickly then that of the U. S. This is demonstrated in Table 12.

This upward trend in incomes would be expected, as better paying white collar jobs become more important (quantitatively) in relation to industrial blue collar jobs. This is also reinforced by the fact that wages and the wage package of the government sector (principally the State) have been increasing rapidly as compared to private industry.
The median family income in the State in 1960 was $5,719. In 1970, the median family income rose to $9,558, an increase of 67 percent over 1960. In real terms, correcting for inflationary effects, the growth would be appreciably slower. In 1970, however, median family income in Harrisburg was only $8,176 or 83 percent of the State average. This is compared to the average median family income of $9,077 for other central cities in the State.
